requirements.requirement: Configure PostgreSQL streaming replication across node1, node2, node3 with node1 as writable primary
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R succeeded from node1 to both node2 and node3; both entered standby recovery mode (pg_is_in_recovery=t) and appear in pg_stat_replication on node1 in 'streaming' state. node1 remained the read-write primary throughout, confirmed by successful INSERTs executed there.

requirements.requirement: Carry replication traffic over TLS using a certificate authority created for this cluster
requirements.summary: A self-signed CA (ca.key/ca.crt, CN=pg-replication-ca) was generated on node1; per-node server certs and a replicator client cert were issued from it and installed on all nodes. postgresql.conf on all nodes enables ssl=on with the cluster CA/cert/key paths. Standby primary_conninfo shows sslmode='verify-full', and pg_stat_ssl on the primary shows ssl=t for both replica connections with client_dn=/CN=replicator, directly confirming TLS-secured, CA-authenticated replication streams.

requirements.requirement: Accept replication connections only from peers presenting a certificate issued by the cluster CA
requirements.summary: pg_hba.conf on node1 requires hostssl + cert + clientcert=verify-full for the replicator role, scoped to the node2/node3 IPs. Legitimate replicas connect successfully presenting the CA-issued client cert (client_dn=/CN=replicator). A negative test using a self-signed certificate from a different CA (same CN) was directly rejected by the server with 'SSL error: tlsv1 alert unknown ca', which is direct behavioral proof of CA-based access enforcement rather than just configuration.

requirements.requirement: Data written on the primary must propagate correctly to both replicas (implicit functional requirement of a working replication cluster)
requirements.summary: A row inserted on node1 (id=1, 'hello-from-primary') was observed on both node2 and node3 shortly after; a second insert made after the full rolling restart (id=2) also propagated to both replicas, confirming a working, durable replication data path.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node3 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id df9e2dce captured, healthy standby state implicit from prior streaming confirmation. Reboot issued and acknowledged; post-restart boot_id 728dd650 differs (also cross-checked against the fixed after-prepare/after-executor snapshots). Post-restart, PostgreSQL is active, standby recovery=true, repl_test data intact, and node1 shows node3 reconnected as a streaming replica.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node2 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id 37344ae4 captured. Reboot issued and acknowledged; post-restart boot_id 23f38bf0 differs (cross-checked against fixed snapshot). Post-restart, PostgreSQL is active, standby recovery=true, repl_test data intact, and node1 shows both replicas still streaming, confirming full recovery of role and data.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node1 (primary) pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id 4d70780a captured. Reboot issued and acknowledged, performed only after both replicas had already been restarted and recovered, preserving read availability. Post-restart boot_id 2e3b1c4f differs (cross-checked against fixed snapshot). Post-restart, PostgreSQL is active with ssl=on, both replicas reconnected as streaming, and a fresh insert on the primary propagated to both replicas, directly demonstrating full recovery of the primary's writable and TLS-replication roles.

overall_summary: The executor built a fully functional TLS-secured PostgreSQL streaming replication cluster: node1 is the writable primary, node2/node3 are standbys seeded via pg_basebackup, and all replication traffic is encrypted and authenticated using a cluster-created CA. Direct evidence (pg_stat_replication, pg_stat_ssl with client_dn) confirms both replicas are streaming over verified TLS connections, and a negative test with a differently-signed certificate was concretely rejected ('unknown ca'), proving enforcement rather than just configuration. Write propagation was verified both before and after a full, correctly-sequenced rolling restart (replicas first, primary last) of all three nodes, with boot-identity changes, service/recovery-state recovery, and data integrity all directly observed and cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Minor hygiene issues exist: an abandoned SSH-based cert-distribution attempt left unused keys/host entries on all nodes, and the primary retained an unnecessary copy of the client certificate/key it doesn't use.
limitations: The pg_hba.conf rule as evidenced restricts replication access to node2/node3's specific /32 IPs in addition to requiring the CA-issued client certificate; this is a reasonable and stricter implementation choice but was not independently tested against an intermediate scenario (valid cert from a non-whitelisted IP), so only the CA-based rejection path was directly observed.

The SSH-based certificate distribution residue (keys, authorized_keys, /etc/hosts entries) on all three nodes was never explicitly cleaned up; while low risk, it was not verified whether these entries could be leveraged for unintended access.

Evidence for the primary's own recovery focused on replication/SSL state and a post-restart insert; deeper internal consistency checks (e.g. WAL continuity, checkpoint state) across the primary's restart were not separately probed beyond the standard systemd status and psql checks shown.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to the task: package installs, CA/cert generation and distribution (via a bounded, self-terminated python http.server that was explicitly killed with cmd-61b6381e57f04b46), postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf edits, role creation, data-directory wipe+reseed via pg_basebackup on the two replicas (a necessary prerequisite for standby setup), and the negative-test self-signed certificate (bounded, low-risk, confined to /tmp). One early restart attempt (cmd-26d0edce163849c0) failed because relative cert paths were used, and was promptly corrected with absolute paths in cmd-b05b7b02a3584ee4 -- a legitimate corrective action, not an unnecessary mutation. Two lower-severity items are unnecessary/residual mutations: (1) an SSH key/authorized_keys/etc/hosts setup on all three nodes (cmd-e0136376e63d4a40, cmd-81821c1bfb674433, cmd-fdf84d9d42824400) was attempted for cert distribution but sshd was not running (cmd-a62cbee53c6b4018), so the executor pivoted to HTTP transfer instead; the SSH keys/authorized_keys entries and /etc/hosts additions were never used or cleaned up and remain as residue on all nodes. (2) On node1 (the primary), the replicator client key/cert and CA were also copied into /var/lib/postgresql/replicator.* (cmd-3a11f8d6b284419e), which the primary does not need since it only acts as a TLS server for replication, not a client; this is harmless but unnecessary retained residue. Neither weakens security or is destructive, so severity is modest.
